criteria.dispatch_only_revoke: Concentrate lifetime control in dispatch by revoking in its finally on all paths, keeping one obvious boundary at the price of killing handled tokens ahead of owner-scope drainage.
criteria.server_only_revoke: Confine revocation to the server outer finally after per-request drainage completes, leaving dispatch to abandon bodies only; direct dispatch users outside the server must then revoke on their own or live with tokens that outlast the call.
criteria.split_boundary: Let each layer end what it owns: dispatch abandons unread bodies on every path and revokes tokens on rejected-route paths that admitted no handler, and the server outer boundary revokes handled tokens after drainage in a finally before the response returns; idempotent revoke makes the duplicated coverage benign.

revocation_boundary.instructions: Which placement of revocation ends handled, failed, rejected, upgraded, and unread-body tokens correctly while keeping admitted child work functional?

criteria.silent_idempotent: revokeRequest erases the token from each table and treats unknown, forged, or already-revoked input as a no-op, staying safe for finally blocks and for the overlapping dispatch-plus-server calls on rejected server requests.
criteria.throw_unknown: revokeRequest signals the resource-state failure whenever input is unknown or already revoked, turning double revocation and forged calls into loud errors that each call site must rule out in advance.

revoke_failure_mode.instructions: Should the revokeRequest primitive ignore or reject unknown and already-revoked input?

state.lifetime_requirements: Sequencing is non-negotiable: settle the handler and materialize its response or upgrade verdict, abandon any unread live body, drain the per-request owner scope with its admitted child work, then revoke the token in an outer finally before the native response is returned. Operations retained past that point across headers, bodies, snapshots, and upgrades must fail with the resource-state failure, yet exclusively past that point: child work using the token mid-drainage has to succeed. Revocation covers buffered requests together with lazy ones, and both handler faults and route rejections must be incapable of leaking a live token.
state.mandate: Can has no external users and its agent authors owe nothing to earlier spellings or generated layouts. The present task shuts down the server request capability following body cleanup and owner drainage. Only two mechanism points are open for advice: the revocation split between dispatch and the server edge, and the revoke primitive failure mode. Ground every judgment in the evidence given below; you can neither read the repository nor execute anything.
state.production_paths: Production ingress turns the native request into a frozen token, attaches the upgrade server, runs serveSnapshot under exactly one per-request owner scope (action match or legacy dispatch into the handler), renders the handler value as a native response, abandons unread live bodies, drains the scope, and sends the response while freeing server leases. Separately, tests and harnesses drive dispatch straight, outside any server scope. Rejecting a route for an unknown path or wrong method launches no handler, so no occupant of that scope can ever have captured the token. Upgrading to WebSocket grabs the native request plus server mid-handler, parks the socket and server object on the session rather than the token, and produces a sentinel in place of an HTTP reply. Shutdown behavior keeps leases whole and closes a single time; the dispatch boundary passes to a later captured-routes task, which demands a tight, explicit edit.
state.token_mechanism: A request is a frozen empty object that keys four WeakMaps: an immutable snapshot of head plus body, a body cell containing either buffered bytes or a live one-shot wire stream, a possibly attached upgrade server, and a set of claimed upgrades. Abandonment just cancels one unread live body stream and keeps all four tables whole, which is why buffered and lazy tokens both survive recognition checks after abandonment; a Bun 1.4.2 probe chaining snapshot, abandon, and re-read proves the point. Each header, body, snapshot, and upgrade entry point consults those tables up front and throws the resource-state failure for unfamiliar keys, meaning removal of a token from every table retracts the whole capability atomically.
